q: In a T-beam under positive moment, what carries the compression?
o: The slab flange over the beam
The web below the neutral axis
n: Positive moment puts the top of the beam in compression. The slab cast with the beam gives a wide compression flange, so the neutral axis usually stays in the slab and little concrete is needed.

q: In SI units, what is the balanced steel ratio ρb of a rectangular beam?
n: 600/(600 + fy) comes from the strain triangle with εcu = 0.003 and Es = 200,000 MPa. The older English-unit form uses 87,000/(87,000 + fy) with fy in psi.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to shear and torsion?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 421.2.1 Strength reduction factors φ
n: Shear and torsion failures are brittle, so φ = 0.75. The older code used 0.85.

q: A beam's main bars are all near its bottom face, and it has no compression bars. What kind of beam is it?
n: A singly reinforced beam has main steel only in the tension zone and relies on the concrete for compression. Top bars that only hold stirrups (hangers) are not counted as compression steel.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a beam or ribbed one-way slab that is continuous at both ends, with a span of 6.3 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/21: 6.3 m / 21 = 300 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to bending of a tension-controlled section?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 421.2.1 Strength reduction factors φ
n: Tension-controlled sections (εt ≥ 0.005) get the highest factor, 0.90, because the steel yields and warns before failure.

q: What happens first in an under-reinforced beam as it is overloaded?
n: The steel yields first, the beam deflects and cracks visibly, and only later does the concrete crush. That warning is why design aims for under-reinforced sections.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a solid one-way slab that is continuous at both ends, with a span of 4.2 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/28: 4.2 m / 28 = 150 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: In strength design, what is Mu?
o: The factored moment the section must resist
The nominal moment strength of the section
The moment that first cracks the concrete
n: Mu comes from the factored loads (such as 1.2D + 1.6L). The section is adequate when φMn ≥ Mu.

q: A beam 300 mm wide with an effective depth of 500 mm has 1,500 mm² of tension steel. What is its steel ratio ρ?
Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to bearing on concrete?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 421.2.1 Strength reduction factors φ
n: Bearing, such as a column or base plate pressing on a footing, gets φ = 0.65. The older code used 0.70.

q: What is a doubly reinforced beam?
o: A beam with two layers of tension bars
A beam with both tension and compression reinforcement
n: Compression bars near the top add moment capacity when the depth is limited and also reduce long-term deflection.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a cantilever beam that is a cantilever, with a span of 2.0 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/8: 2.0 m / 8 = 250 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to axial tension?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 421.2.1 Strength reduction factors φ
n: Members in axial tension, and tension with bending, are tension-controlled and get 0.90.

q: Why do codes want flexural members to be tension-controlled?
o: It uses the least amount of steel
It makes the beam as stiff as possible
Yielding steel gives warning before collapse
It prevents all cracking in service
n: Ductile failure lets people notice trouble and leave. NSCP rewards it with φ = 0.90 and limits beams to εt ≥ 0.004 so they cannot be over-reinforced.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a solid one-way cantilever slab that is a cantilever, with a span of 1.5 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/10: 1.5 m / 10 = 150 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: In a simply supported beam under gravity load, where is the concrete in compression?
o: At the top of the beam
At the bottom of the beam
Nowhere; it is all in tension
n: Positive moment bends the beam concave up: the top is in compression and the bottom in tension, where the main bars go.

q: How does NSCP 2015 limit the maximum steel in a beam?
o: By limiting ρ to 0.75 times ρb
By requiring a net tensile strain εt ≥ 0.004
By limiting ρ to 0.5% of bd
By limiting the bars to four per layer
n: Older codes used ρmax = 0.75ρb. Since ACI 318-02, and in NSCP 2015, the limit is set by strain: εt ≥ 0.004 for beams, and εt ≥ 0.005 to get φ = 0.90.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to tied compression members (compression-controlled)?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 421.2.1 Strength reduction factors φ
n: Compression-controlled tied columns get 0.65, the lowest factor, because they fail by crushing with little warning. The older code used 0.70.

q: When is a doubly reinforced beam used?
o: When the beam is unusually deep
When the beam carries no load
When the beam is a cantilever only
When the depth is limited and more moment is needed
n: If architectural limits cap the depth, adding compression steel lets the section carry more moment while staying ductile.

q: When may a designer use a thinner beam or slab than the NSCP minimum-thickness table allows?
o: When computed deflections are within the limits
Whenever the owner agrees in writing
Whenever f'c is higher than 21 MPa
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The table is a shortcut to avoid deflection calculations. A thinner member is allowed if computed immediate and long-term deflections meet the NSCP limits.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what strength reduction factor φ applies to spirally reinforced compression members (compression-controlled)?
ref: NSCP 2015 Table 421.2.1 Strength reduction factors φ
n: Spiral columns get 0.75, higher than tied columns (0.65), because the spiral confines the core and makes failure more ductile.

q: What happens first in an over-reinforced beam as it is overloaded?
o: The concrete crushes before the steel yields
The beam slides off its support
n: With too much steel, the concrete reaches its crushing strain of 0.003 while the steel is still elastic. The failure is sudden, so the code does not allow it.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a simply supported beam that is simply supported, with a span of 6.4 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/16: 6.4 m / 16 = 400 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: A beam carries a dead load moment of 40 kN·m and a live load moment of 25 kN·m. What is the factored moment using U = 1.2D + 1.6L?
n: Mu = 1.2(40) + 1.6(25) = 48 + 40 = 88 kN·m. Also check U = 1.4D = 56 kN·m; 88 kN·m governs.
steps: Check 1.4D = 56 kN·m, smaller, so 88 kN·m governs

q: Using fy = 275 MPa and f'c = 21 MPa, what is the minimum steel ratio of a beam under NSCP 2015?
n: ρmin is the larger of 0.25√f'c/fy = 0.25 × 4.58 / 275 = 0.0042 and 1.4/fy = 1.4 / 275 = 0.0051. The larger, 0.0051, governs.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a solid one-way slab that is simply supported, with a span of 3.0 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/20: 3.0 m / 20 = 150 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: Why does a beam cast with its slab act as a T-beam?
o: Because the beam is shaped like a T in plan
Because its bars are bent into T shapes
Because it supports a T-shaped load
Slab and beam are monolithic, so the slab acts as a flange
n: Monolithic casting joins slab and beam. NSCP limits how much slab counts (the effective flange width), based on span, slab thickness and beam spacing.

q: What is a balanced section?
o: Steel yields just as the concrete reaches 0.003
Top and bottom steel have equal areas
The neutral axis lies at mid-depth
Dead and live loads are equal
n: The balanced condition marks the boundary between ductile (under-reinforced) and brittle (over-reinforced) behaviour. Design stays well on the ductile side.

q: What value of β1 applies to concrete with f'c = 21 MPa?
n: β1 is 0.85 for f'c up to 28 MPa, then drops by 0.05 for each 7 MPa above 28, but not below 0.65. It sets the depth of the equivalent stress block, a = β1c.

q: What is the real reason an over-reinforced beam fails without warning?
o: There is no concrete in the compression zone
The compression concrete crushes while the steel is still elastic
n: The concrete is there, but it reaches its crushing strain before the steel yields. Because the steel never yields, there is no large deflection to warn anyone.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a beam or ribbed one-way slab that is continuous at one end, with a span of 5.55 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/18.5: 5.55 m / 18.5 = 300 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.

q: A beam has a nominal moment strength of 200 kN·m and is tension-controlled. What is its design moment strength?
n: φMn = 0.90 × 200 = 180 kN·m. The beam is adequate if the factored moment Mu is no more than 180 kN·m.

q: What net tensile strain makes a section tension-controlled under NSCP 2015?
n: At εt ≥ 0.005 the steel has stretched well past yield (about 0.002 for Grade 60), so φ = 0.90. Between the yield strain and 0.005 the section is in transition and φ drops toward 0.65.

q: Under NSCP 2015, what minimum thickness applies to a solid one-way slab that is continuous at one end, with a span of 3.6 m, when deflections are not computed?
ref: NSCP 2015 Tables 407.3.1.1 (one-way slabs) and 409.3.1.1 (beams), normal-weight concrete, fy = 420 MPa
n: The limit for this case is L/24: 3.6 m / 24 = 150 mm. The table applies to members not supporting partitions likely to be damaged by deflection.
